passages.happening:
Zedekiah was twenty-one when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem (verse 1). He did evil in the LORD's sight, as Jehoiakim had (verse 2). ‘For because of the anger of the LORD, all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until He finally banished them from His presence’ (verse 3). And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

The siege began in the tenth month of his ninth year (verse 4). By the fourth month of his eleventh year the famine was so severe there was no food, and the city wall was breached (verses 6 and 7). Zedekiah fled and was captured in the plains of Jericho (verse 8). At Riblah the king of Babylon passed sentence on him, had his sons and the officials of Judah killed, blinded him, and took him to Babylon, where he was kept in prison until he died (verses 9 to 11). The chapter states this plainly in a few lines, and these notes do the same.

In the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year, Nebuzaradan entered Jerusalem (verse 12). ‘He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem’ (verse 13). The army broke down the walls (verse 14). He took the people into exile, leaving some of the poorest to tend vineyards and fields (verses 15 and 16). The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars, the stands and the bronze sea of the temple and carried everything to Babylon (verses 17 to 23). The chief priest Seraiah and other leaders were taken to Riblah and put to death (verses 24 to 27). ‘So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is a historical appendix, close to 2 Kings 24 and 25. Chapter 51 ended with here end the words of Jeremiah, so chapter 52 shows how everything he said came true.

The dates are given with care. Zedekiah was put on the throne in 597 BC and rebelled hoping for Egypt's help. The siege began about January 588 BC and ended when the wall was breached in the summer of 587 or 586 BC. Zedekiah fled toward the Jordan valley and was taken to Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters at Riblah on the Orontes River in Syria. A month later Nebuzaradan burned the temple, the palace and the city.

The long list of temple bronzes in verses 17 to 23 is a list of loss. Solomon's great works were broken up for their metal. The first hearers would know each piece by name.
passages.later: Kings tells the same story in almost the same words (2 Kings 25:1-21). Lamentations grieves it from inside the ruins, and still says, ‘Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed’ (Lamentations 3:22).
passages.asks: The book ends by telling again the disaster Jeremiah warned of for forty years. Ask why it matters to remember a catastrophe honestly, without softening it. And ask what you would need to hear after a loss like this.

passages.t: The numbers of the exiles, and a king released
passages.happening:
These are the people Nebuchadnezzar carried away: ‘in the seventh year, 3,023 Jews’ (verse 28), ‘in Nebuchadnezzar’s eighteenth year, 832 people from Jerusalem’ (verse 29), and in his twenty-third year, 745 more (verse 30). ‘So in all, 4,600 people were taken away’ (verse 30).

In the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, in the first year of Evil-merodach king of Babylon, the king pardoned Jehoiachin and released him from prison (verse 31). ‘And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon’ (verse 32). ‘So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life’ (verse 33). The king of Babylon gave him a daily portion for the rest of his life, until the day of his death (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
These figures, found only in Jeremiah, are smaller than the ten thousand that 2 Kings 24:14 gives for the first deportation, and readers explain the difference in more than one way. The three waves were in 597 BC, in 587 or 586 BC, and in 582 or 581 BC, the last perhaps a reprisal after Gedaliah's murder.

Evil-merodach, in Babylonian Amel-Marduk, was Nebuchadnezzar's son and reigned from 562 to 560 BC. The release of Jehoiachin came in 561 BC. Cuneiform ration tablets dug up at Babylon, from the 590s BC, list rations of oil for Jehoiachin king of Judah and his sons, showing that the captive king lived as a royal hostage fed by the Babylonian court.

The book ends quietly. A king of David's line takes off his prison clothes and eats at a foreign king's table. It is a small light. The line of David has been humbled, but it has not ended, and God's promise to David is still alive.
passages.later: Kings ends with the same scene: ‘the king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life’ (2 Kings 25:30). Matthew's genealogy carries the line on from him: ‘Jeconiah was the father of Shealtiel’ (Matthew 1:12).
passages.hard:
Jeremiah said none of Jehoiachin's offspring would sit on David's throne (22:30). How then does Matthew trace Jesus' line through him?

Jeremiah 22:30 says no descendant of Jehoiachin would prosper on David's throne ruling in Judah, and none did: his grandson Zerubbabel became governor under Persia, not king. Christian interpreters offer several answers. Some note that Matthew traces Jesus' legal descent through Joseph, while Jesus was not Joseph's biological son, so the sentence on Jehoiachin's physical descendants does not strictly apply. Others observe that Haggai 2:23 reverses the picture of 22:24, calling Zerubbabel God's signet ring, which suggests the judgment on the line was not permanent. Others add that Jesus does not reign from an earthly throne in Judah but from the right hand of God. Jewish tradition also discussed whether Jehoiachin's repentance in exile softened the decree.

The question has several reasonable answers, and they can be held together.
passages.asks: The book ends with a captive king changing out of his prison clothes. Ask what small sign of God's faithfulness you could hold on to after a long loss. And ask what it means that God's promise survived even when the throne was gone.
